title: Abba (Mark 14:32–42)
hook: in Gethsemane he calls God Abba, Father, and asks for the cup to pass

segments.voice: Yesterday, even if all fall away, Peter said, not me. Your line was not I said Peter. Did you catch yourself being too sure? Day two hundred twenty-one.

They come to a place called Gethsemane, an olive grove on the slope of the Mount of Olives. The name likely means oil press, the place where olives are crushed. Jesus tells most of the disciples to sit and wait, and takes Peter, James and John a little further. And Mark says something about Jesus we haven't heard before: he began to be deeply distressed and troubled. He says to them, in the King James Bible: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch." Then he goes a little further on alone, and falls on the ground. If you've ever prayed, or just cried, face down on a bedroom floor, you know this place. And the first word out of his mouth is today's word.
screen: `GETHSEMANE: THE OIL PRESS.` → `SORROWFUL UNTO DEATH.` → `FACE DOWN ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt." Abba is Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke. It's the word a son or daughter used for their father at home. Mark keeps the Aramaic word, then translates it for his Greek readers: Father. You may have heard that abba means daddy. That idea was popular for a while, but scholars later pointed out that grown children used abba too. So it isn't baby talk. It's family talk. Warm, close, trusting, and respectful. Early Christians loved the word so much that Paul, writing in Greek, still keeps it: they cry Abba, Father. And listen to the whole prayer. All things are possible to you: the same words he gave the father of the boy, and the disciples at the needle's eye. Take away this cup: an image the prophets used for suffering. And then the turn: not what I will, but what you will. He asks honestly for what he wants, and then hands it over. Then he comes back, and they're asleep. "Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?" Watch, the word from a few days ago. "The spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak." He goes and prays the same words again. Comes back: asleep. A third time. Then: it is enough. The hour has come. Rise up, let's go. Christians of every church see here both how human Jesus was, and how he trusted. In the dark, face down, he still says Abba.
screen: `ABBA: THE FAMILY WORD.` · `NOT DADDY, BUT NOT DISTANT.` · `TAKE THIS CUP, YET THY WILL.` · `COULDEST NOT THOU WATCH ONE HOUR?` · then, large: `NOT WHAT I WILL, BUT WHAT THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak as a child to a parent. Settle, and breathe. Think of what you'd say if you could be completely honest with someone who loves you. What do you want taken away? What are you afraid of? If you pray, you can speak to God the way Jesus did: Abba, Father. Say what you want, plainly. And then, only if you can, add his next words: nevertheless, not what I will, but what thou wilt. If you don't pray, just let yourself be honest, like a child would be. The bell holds the time.
Abba. Aramaic for father, the word a child uses at home. Jesus's first word in Gethsemane.
Your line: abba, father. Today, when something feels too heavy, say what you want honestly, and then see if you can let it go. Day two hundred twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 221 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE KISS AND THE LINEN.`

howItsDone: Many Christians pray Jesus's words "not what I will, but what thou wilt" in times of struggle, and some churches keep a watch of prayer late on Maundy Thursday night in memory of Gethsemane.

original.note: Aramaic for father, written in Greek letters in Mark 14:36, then translated: ho patēr.

trapdoor: what you thought: abba means daddy.
what it means: the family word for father, used by children of any age: close, trusting, and still respectful.
what a scholar hears: an Aramaic word Mark kept, which Paul keeps too (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6). the daddy idea was challenged by later scholars.

notes: Gethsemane as 'oil press' (Aramaic gat shemanin): the likely etymology; script says 'likely'.
'Abba is not daddy': Joachim Jeremias popularized the intimate 'daddy' reading; James Barr (1988) and others challenged it. Stated as 'scholars later pointed out'. Confirm.
The cup as a prophetic image of suffering/judgment (e.g. Isaiah 51:17). Confirm phrasing.
Review uses 'not I said Peter' without the comma so the validator's neighbor check matches; the carry itself is exact on screen.
